description.narrative: The UNICEF programme offers a multi-sectoral approach, where focus is placed on improving access to basic social services and improve the beneficiaries’ ability to address basic needs. The main beneficiaries of the contribution are children and adolescents from both the internally displaced populations and the host communities, although targeted communities at large should benefit from the results of the activities. The contribution will focus on cash payments through Mozambique’s national social security system, as well as on providing support to services that will increase access to basic health, water and sanitation and nutrition. Education will also be prioritized through the provision of Temporary Learning Spaces, and Multi-Purpose Centres will be set up where vocational training, psychosocial support and various community activities will be provided. The aim of such is to support children and youth to realise their rights, increase their chances of a better future and make them less susceptible to recruitment into armed groups.

UNICEF:s program är holistiskt och multisektoriellt, där fokus ligger på att förbättra tillgången till grundläggande samhällstjänster och förbättra mottagarnas förmåga att adressera basala behov. Huvudsakliga mottagare för stödet är barn och ungdomar ur både internflykting- samt värdbefolkningen, även om samhällena där de bor även i stort kommer att kunna dra nytta av resultaten av aktiviteterna. Stödet kommer till stor del fokusera på kontantbaserade utbetalningar genom landets nationella socialförsäkringssystem för att ge mottagarna möjlighet att utöka sitt matintag och förbättra sin nutritionsstatus, samt bistå med stöd till utökad tillgång till basal hälsovård, vatten- och sanitet samt nutritionslära. Även utbildning kommer att prioriteras genom tillhandahållande av temporära utbildningslokaler för att säkra barn- och ungdomars tillgång till utbildning, samt upprättandet av barn- och ungdomscenter för bl a fortbildning, psykosocialt stöd och olika pedagogiska aktiviteter för att stödja deras välmående, framtidsutsikter och roll i samhället, samt minska risken för att de rekryteras av väpnade grupper aktiva i området.

The general objective of the intervention is the fulfillment of child rights for vulnerable children, either living as IDP:s or in affected host communities, and is based on work within three main pillars; 1) children survive and thrive: the first 1000 days; 2) children learn and are protected from exploitation, abuse and violence; and 3) vulnerable adolescents access adequate support services. The specific goal as set out in the results framework is "to support conflict-affected children from birth through 18 and their caregivers with a comprehensive community-based package of services.

sector.narrative: Multisector aid for basic social services

title.narrative: Decision on Agreement UNICEF Nexus Support

description.narrative:
Outcome 1: Children survive and thrive in the first 1000 days through access to an integrated lifesaving package of quality series.
Examples of reached results include: 104 965 vulnerable IDP children, pregnant and breastfeeding women have accessed health consultations in UNICEF-supported facilities (target 89 200); 224 706 children under the age of 5 were screened for malnutrition (target 200 000) and 2 352 severely malnourished children were admitted for treatment (target 2 000).
On the latter, UNICEF noted in a previous report that due to increased violence and disruption to health services in the project's implementation areas the goal of 2 000 may not be met before the end of the activity period. Thus it was a welcome result that UNICEF managed to reach the full amount of children (and more) than planned for, given the great need for intervention in the area.
The reason for the massive reach in regards to health services UNICEF largely attributed to their partnerships and the deployment of integrated mobile brigades, which significantly expanded access to health care in remote and under served areas such as Mazeze and Chiúre Velho, which were two areas badly affected by insecurity. 205 outreach visits took place to communities without regular access to health care, engaging local health workers and activists.
The use of mobile brigades also had the positive effect of strengthening the connection between health facilities, outreach teams and communities, and managed to optimize available resources to improve sustainability. For instance, these partnerships sought to enhance the impact of social behaviour change messages by collaborating with other initiatives in the target communities.
With the Swedish support, UNICEF partnered with local health authorities to enhance the delivery of critical maternal and neonatal child health (MNCH) services. UNICEF procured critical medical equipment for the care of sick newborns (incl. 19 newborn cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) kits, incubators, and resuscitation tables), supporting care for around 25 000 newborns in 20 health facilities. Health care workers were also trained to use the kits, and received training on integrated management on childhood illnesses.
Under outcome 1, the component connected to the Child Grant programme was included. This component allowed for social security payments through the state social protection system. The target was to have between 2 000 and 2 760 children aged 0-2 years old enrolled in the project by the end of the project period. In total UNICEF facilitated the registration 7 668 beneficiaries, of which 2 760 were covered under this project. Given the challenging situation in Cabo Delgado, where the delegations had to start distributing payments on non-regular basis (every 4-5 months) to enhance logistical planning and reduce transportation of large sums of money every month to payment points (and in particular in districts like Macomia where funds needed to be transported all the way from Pemba due to limited banking facilities on site), delays were seen to the payments. This meant that the enrolled children could not receive the full 24 month transfer in the grant duration. Instead, the Swedish funding was redistributed to an additional 1 415 children, bringing the case load reached under this contribution to 4 175 children for 15 months, rather than 2 760 over 24 months. To complete the state decided 24 month cycle of the child grant, the remaining 9 months of transfers will be covered through other grants, for instance from the German development bank KfW.
The Child Grant component of the project has encountered a number of challenges since its start, with delays from the outset owing to difficulties in agreeing with authorities on chosen modality - which at the beginning of the project was meant to be the post-emergency payment related to displacement - and later, once the child grant was chosen, agreeing on the geographical locations. However, bringing the child grant to highly vulnerable areas, can be seen as a great achievement, and Sida is pleased to have participated in the funding thereof.
Outcome 2: Children learn and are protected from exploitation, abuse and violence
Examples of reached results include: 20 600 children received access to educational services (exceeding the target of 10 000), through provision of teaching and leaning materials as distributed by district authorities. 3 200 children gained access to education services through 32 Temporary Learning Spaces (TLSs) installed in14 schools. Apart from accommodating 3 200 children, this eased the heavy pressure of overcrowded classrooms which followed the vast displacement wave with an influx of over 100 000 IDPs to the area. Although the target on TLS was reached, it was a reduction (as agreed in a previous programme revision) to the initial plan of number of TLSs that was to be constructed. The reduction had to be done to accommodate for increased construction costs and reduced available funds due to unfavorable exchange rate fluctuations. The increased construction costs were due to increased pricing in the supply chains and materials, which was a phenomenon seen globally post-Covid. The learner supplies were distributed by district authorities and reached 51 schools across Ancuabe and Chiure.
In partnership with the Provincial Directorate of Education, the Teacher Training Institute and the Education, Youth and Technology District Services, UNICEF provided training to 200 teachers on teachers roles in crisis contexts, including how to adjust pedagogical methodologies, the protection and provision of Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) to students, Gender Based Violence (GBV), Violence Against Children (VAC) and Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). These trainings were particularly relevant considering the large insecurity and displacement which took place across Ancuabe and Chiure during 2024, when over 20 schools were either damaged or destroyed due to armed conflict and post electoral violence.
19 519 parents and care givers participated in dialogues on VAC. The target was 7 000, but this was heavily reduced in the last programme revision (and included in the last reporting period) to better align with UNICEF's targets in their Humanitarian Appeal for Children (HAC) which was based on more accurate estimates for Ancuabe and Chiure.
Additionally, 8 430 parents and caregivers (target 1 500) and 20 608 children (target 13 000) accessed community based protection services (support to children affected by violence to access protective services, such as social services and access to safe learning environments) and basic MHPSS (for the caregivers). 13 864 children (target 800) were identified as in need of case management due to different vulnerabilities, including support for family tracing and reunification for unaccompanied children, and for reintegration of children associated with armed groups. UNICEF identified 364 unaccompanied or separated children (180 girls and 184 boys), 35 % of which they managed to reunite with their primary care giver, and the remaining children having been placed in foster homes. Despite having exceeded the target due to needs arising out of considerable population movements (notably attacks in Chiure in February 2024), these services continued due to the vast need in the area. Through community based child protection committees, UNICEF and partners also led awareness raising efforts on prevention of child abuse, exploitation, and early marriage, and managed to refer 1 189 children to education, birth registration and health services.
13 child friendly Multi-Purpose Community-based protection centres (MPCs) (basic centres set up with a purpose to provide a safe space to serve a variety of functions for community-based healing and resilience building) were constructed. The MPCs activities were based on a model approved by the Provincial Social Affairs Service, the Provincial Department of Gender, Children and Social Action and the District Health Women and Social Action Services, and function as an entry point to identify children in need of specialised support. The target was 15, but UNICEF was unable to meet this due to two factors; a) two planned locations were deemed too insecure and UNCIEF instead set up two large tents that could be used for a variety of functions, including provision of focused MHPSS, and b) UNICEF's chosen partner delivered substandard constructions, which meant that UNICEF had to transfer activities to a new partner mid-programme, which meant that the reaching the full target was not possible. However, despite delays in the process, UNICEF managed to conduct their planned activities in various community spaces, including through mobile brigades and through working in open spaces whilst awaiting completion of the structures. Activities in the MPCs included psycho-social support, case management, recreational activities, referrals to other services, life skills sessions, art therapy, counselling and sports.
15 toilet blocks were built to accommodate five TLSs and ten MPCs, and 76 500 children in 51 schools benefited from the distribution of 153 school hygiene kits.
Under outcome 2 UNICEF reported on their collaboration with the Dallarie institute and Ministry of Defence (MoD) on the prevention of recruitment and use of children in armed conflict. Within the collaborative framework between Dallaire-MoD-UNICEF on the prevention of recruitment and use of children, a technical working group was established, and coordination meetings held to facilitate the capacity building programme of the Mozambican forces and military training institutions, including the development and validation of a training guide (course outline and facilitators modules tailored for the mozambican armed forces). As a result, 1 551 mozambican soldiers were trained on child protection principles, the six grave violations against children and appropriate procedures for identifying and referring children associated with armed groups. UNICEF's high level advocacy and engagement with the MoD also led to a draft handover protocol and the establishment of child protection units within the military.
Outcome 3: Vulnerable adolescents access adequate support services
Examples of reached results include: 1 586 out of school adolescents and youth aged 12 to 18 benefited from literacy, numeracy and skills training (target 1 500, reduced in an earlier revision) as delivered by community school teachers and local crafts people (through partnership between UNICEF and the Education Youth and Technology District Services). Many of these individuals had never attended school before, or had dropped out in early ages, thus lacking foundational literacy and numeracy skills. After six months of learning basic reading and math skills, the participants started training in their preferred vocations. The vocational training included carpentry, tailoring, mechanics, weaving, and artisanry. The training also encompassed practical instruction in financial literacy and small business management techniques. Upon completion of the courses, the participants were either given start up kits or supported to participate in internship opportunities (approximately 100 participants were referred to internship opportunities through leveraging activities of another UNICEF project in Chiure with complementing funds). The start up kits were shared by several participants, encouraging them to establish small cooperatives.
Due to the increase in violence and displacement during the project period, especially in Chiure district, the literacy, numeracy, and vocational training activities faced interruptions in 2024 spanning several weeks, both in February-March and again in April-May. Additionally, the volatile situation caused delays in the start of a new cohort of participants, as some of the communities selected for the program were inaccessible due to insecurity, which in the end forced a change of target communities.
27 434 children and adolescents, including children with disabilities, benefited from MHPSS services in safe spaces (the MPCs, tents and open spaces noted above). This is more than double the target of 12 000 individuals, and was managed to surpass targets by such an amount due to the introduction of mobile child protection teams in Chiure district. During 2023, UNICEF and partners also adopted a more nuanced approach to MHPSS in Cabo Delgado, shifting from primarily recreational activities to a diversified approach ensuring that activities were tailored to groups based on age and gender, where appropriate. The activities were also provided in smaller groups on a three month cycle, which allowed the participants to engage in skills and resilience-building sessions regularly which, according to the report, had a greater impact on program quality.
Connected to outcome 3, UNICEF conducted a market analysis on job opportunities for adolescents and youth to inform future learning opportunities in various districts of Cabo Delgado. Not surprisingly, the study found that the number of training providers and employment opportunities - especially in the formal market - in Cabo Delgado is very limited and mainly concentrated to Pemba, highlighting the need for authorities to better coordinate training and employment opportunities. Recommendations also included and enhanced inclusion of Communication Technology (ICT) skills within programmes and diversified vocational training courses that align more closely with local contexts. Sida has requested that the findings of this market analysis is used in the planning of project Planit 16627 "WFP/UNICEF Conflict prevention & child protection in Cabo Delgado".
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
